skuLines.line: Toor / arhar dal — economy grade, sold loose
skuLines.examples: Loose mill-grade toor dal (Indore/Latur origin), Bharat Dal toor, unbranded 30kg sack broken to loose
skuLines.packSizes: loose by weight (250g-5kg), plus own-pack 1kg / 2kg pouches
skuLines.seasonality: year-round; small lift Oct-Feb when whole pulses take share
skuLines.notes: Aug-2026 mandi anchor ~Rs 82/kg (commodityonline / kisandeals). Loose sale is GST-nil and carries the best margin, but an open sack in 70-90% monsoon RH infests with pulse beetle in 2-3 weeks — buy in 30kg lots not 500kg, strict FIFO, neem/bay-leaf sachets.

skuLines.examples: Tata Sampann Toor Dal, bb Royal / Good Life Toor Dal, Rajdhani Toor Dal, Fortune Toor Dal
skuLines.notes: Pre-packaged and labelled packs up to 25kg attract 5% GST; margin is thin (2-8% on branded staples) so this line exists for trust/quality, not profit. Toor is the single most-bought dal in Indian grocery.

skuLines.examples: Tata Sampann Unpolished Toor Dal, Organic Tattva Arhar Dal, 24 Mantra Organic Tur Dal, Madhi / bold 7mm+ grade
skuLines.notes: Unpolished = no oil/water/leather polish; the fastest-growing premium tier in modern trade. One facing is enough on a campus store — buyers here are salaried, not affluent.

skuLines.line: Toor dal — oily (madhi) grade for long holding
skuLines.examples: Nirav Desi Madhi Toor Dal (oily), Pari brand oiled toor, oiled toor 30kg sack
skuLines.seasonality: stock deliberately before the Jul-Sep monsoon
skuLines.notes: The oil coat is a natural preservative against infestation — the single most useful grade for a heavy-monsoon hill store holding stock for 3+ months. Must be flagged as oily at the counter; some buyers reject it.

skuLines.line: Chana dal (split Bengal gram) — economy loose
skuLines.examples: Loose chana dal, Bharat Dal chana (subsidised), unbranded 30kg mill sack
skuLines.seasonality: spikes around Gurpurabs and langar days (maa-chole di dal)
skuLines.notes: Aug-2026 mandi anchor ~Rs 74/kg. Half of the langar-dal pair (urad chilka + chana dal), so a Sikh institution's canteens and staff kitchens both pull it — never let it go out of stock.

skuLines.examples: Tata Sampann Chana Dal, Tata Sampann Organic Unpolished Chana Dal, Good Life Chana Dal Unpolished, Rajdhani Chana Dal
skuLines.notes: Chana dal is among the highest-protein dals (~10g/100g cooked), which is the claim modern trade now prints on front-of-pack.

skuLines.examples: Tata Sampann Moong Dal Dhuli, Good Life Moong Dal, bb Royal Moong Dal, loose dhuli moong
skuLines.seasonality: year-round; spikes during illness/exam season and post-monsoon stomach complaints
skuLines.notes: The single most versatile dal on this campus: weaning food for babies, the light dal for the elderly and the sick bay, and moong dal halwa/cheela. Lowest gas/allergy risk of any pulse — keep it in stock even when everything else is short.

skuLines.line: Moong dal dhuli — small baby / convalescent pack
skuLines.examples: Own-pack 200g/250g dhuli moong, Tata Sampann Moong Dal 500g, Organic Tattva Moong Dal Yellow Split
skuLines.notes: Married staff families with 6-month-plus babies need moong dal ka pani weekly and will not buy 1kg of it. A 200-250g facing is a real gap-filler in a campus with no chemist-adjacent baby aisle nearby; also avoids the weevil risk of a family holding an open 1kg through monsoon.

skuLines.line: Moong dal chilka (split green gram with skin)
skuLines.examples: Good Life Moong Dal Chhilka, Organic Tattva Moong Dal Green Split, loose chilka moong
skuLines.notes: Higher fibre than dhuli; the everyday North Indian household dal alongside masoor. Distinct SKU — buyers do not substitute chilka for dhuli.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Moong Whole, Organic Tattva Moong Whole, loose sabut moong
skuLines.seasonality: summer and exam months (sprouts); winter for whole-moong dal
skuLines.notes: Doubles as the sprouting SKU — the cheapest protein a hostel student or gym-going staff member can buy. Also the base for the F&V counter's fresh-sprouts line.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Masoor Dal, Good Life Masoor Malka, Tata Sampann Masoor Dal, loose malka
skuLines.notes: Cheapest dal on the shelf (mandi ~Rs 54-58/kg) and the fastest-cooking — which matters on a hill campus where LPG/fuel is hauled in. This is the price-entry dal for the lowest-paid non-teaching staff; never price it up to protect toor.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Masoor Whole, Organic Tattva Masoor Whole, Good Life Masoor Whole Black Unpolished
skuLines.seasonality: peaks Nov-Feb (sabut masoor is a winter dal)
skuLines.notes: Punjabi households cook sabut masoor as a distinct dish, not a substitute for split masoor. Cold Baru Sahib winters push whole-pulse demand up sharply.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Urad Dal, Tata Sampann Unpolished Organic Urad Dal (Dhuli), loose dhuli urad
skuLines.seasonality: spikes around festivals (dahi bhalla, papad/vadi making, idli-dosa batter)
skuLines.notes: Aug-2026 mandi anchor ~Rs 78.5/kg. Also the batter dal for any South Indian staff/students in the university, and for home papad and wadi making.

skuLines.line: Urad dal chilka (split black gram with skin)
skuLines.examples: Good Life Urad Dal Chhilka, loose chilka urad, Organic Tattva Urad Dal Black Split
skuLines.notes: The 'maa' of maa-chole di dal — the canonical gurudwara langar dal, cooked with chana dal. In a Kalgidhar Trust township this is a religious-calendar SKU, not just a grocery one.

skuLines.line: Urad sabut / kali dal (whole black gram)
skuLines.examples: Good Life Urad Whole, Organic Tattva Urad Black Whole, loose sabut urad (mah di dal)
skuLines.seasonality: strong Nov-Feb (dal makhani weather) and for weddings/functions
skuLines.notes: Mah/kali dal is a Himachali as well as a Punjabi staple — black gram has been part of local hill cuisine for centuries. Pairs with rajma as the two winter must-stocks.

skuLines.examples: Rajdhani Kabuli Chana, Good Life Kabuli Chana, Organic Tattva Kabuli Chana, loose kabuli
skuLines.seasonality: heavy at Gurpurabs, langar, weddings, functions; Navratri/Ashtami
skuLines.notes: Aug-2026 mandi anchor ~Rs 81/kg. Chole is the standard function/langar dish — expect large single-purchase spikes ahead of religious dates, so buy against the Trust's event calendar rather than a flat monthly indent.

skuLines.line: Kabuli chana — bold / premium large calibre
skuLines.examples: Rajdhani Kabuli Chana (bold), bb Royal Kabuli Chana 12mm+, Golden Chana premium
skuLines.notes: Bold calibre is a visible quality cue and sells at a real premium for chaat/chole where the chickpea is seen whole. One facing next to the standard grade.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Chana Brown, Organic Tattva Kala Chana, loose kala chana
skuLines.seasonality: Navratri / Ashtami-Kanjak, fasting days, sprouting in summer
skuLines.notes: Three demand streams at once: religious (Ashtami kala chana), sprouts/health, and cheap protein for hostel students. Long shelf life as a whole pulse — the safest thing to stock deep before monsoon.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Rajma Chitra, Rajdhani Rajma Chitra, Organic Tattva Rajma Chitra, loose chitra
skuLines.seasonality: strong Oct-Mar; rajma-chawal is winter food in the hills
skuLines.notes: Mandi anchor ~Rs 122/kg (medium chitra). Rajma-chawal and madra are core Himachali dishes as well as Punjabi — this is arguably the highest-emotion pulse on this campus.

skuLines.line: Rajma lal / small red kidney bean
skuLines.examples: Good Life Rajma Red, Jammu/Kashmiri small red rajma, Good Life Rajma Sharmili
skuLines.notes: Cooks softer and faster than chitra and is the preferred type in many Punjabi homes — genuinely a separate buying decision, not a variant.

skuLines.examples: Chamba Kugti rajma, Bharmour rajma, Pahaari Bazar pahari rajma, local Sirmaur-grown rajma
skuLines.notes: Kugti/Bharmour rajma is a recognised premium hill variety. Two roles: a genuine premium shelf for senior staff and visitors, and a local-procurement story the Trust can own by buying from Sirmaur growers. Supply is small-lot and seasonal — treat as a campaign, not a permanent line.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Cowpea White, Organic Tattva Cowpea White, loose lobia
skuLines.notes: One of the eight dals every Indian kitchen keeps; also a fast-cooking whole pulse, which matters where fuel is expensive.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Moth, Organic Tattva Moth, loose matki
skuLines.notes: Mainly a sprouting pulse here. Small facing; pairs with the sprout-mix line.

skuLines.examples: Good Life White Peas Dry, loose safed matar, Rajdhani Safed Matar
skuLines.seasonality: winter (matar kulcha, chaat); fasting/langar side dishes
skuLines.notes: The cheapest legume on the shelf and a chaat/street-food base — high pull with students and with the canteens. Being cheapest, it is also the substitution SKU when dal prices spike.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Green Peas, loose dried green matar, Rajdhani Green Peas
skuLines.notes: Sits next to safed matar; the two together cover the chaat-and-canteen demand without touching frozen peas.

skuLines.examples: Buraansh Pahadi Kulth, Pahaari Bazar kulth, Kumaon Foods gahat dal, local Chamba kulth
skuLines.notes: A genuinely local Himachali pulse (Chamba, Karsog, Barot), prized for kidney/stone benefits — exactly the kind of thing an off-campus resident cannot easily buy back. High-empathy, low-volume: one small facing, sourced locally.

skuLines.examples: Pahaari Bazar bhatt, Kumaon/Himachali bhatt ki dal, local bhatt
skuLines.notes: Traditional hill pulse (Dolichos/Vigna spp. group) that survives harsh climate; part of the region's functional-food tradition. Stock only if local supply is reliable — no modern-trade source.

skuLines.examples: Val dal, chowli dal, loose val papdi dal
skuLines.notes: Regional (Gujarat/Maharashtra) — only worth a facing if the university has staff or students from those states. Check before buying.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Chana Green, dried hara chana, loose green chana
skuLines.seasonality: winter, when fresh chholiya is in season
skuLines.notes: Competes with fresh chholiya at the F&V counter in winter; only a small dried facing needed.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Dal Mix, Good Life Punjabi Mix Dal, Rajdhani Panchratna Dal, Tata Sampann Mixed Dal
skuLines.notes: The India mixed-dal market is growing on convenience alone. Good for small staff households who cannot justify five open dal jars in a monsoon climate.

skuLines.line: Langar / maa-chole dal blend (urad chilka + chana dal)
skuLines.examples: Good Life Punjabi Mix Dal, Good Life Tadka Mix, own-pack maa-chole blend
skuLines.seasonality: year-round; heavy on Gurpurabs and langar days
skuLines.notes: A pre-blended two-dal pack is the highest-relevance own-brand SKU this store could make: it is the dish the whole township eats. Blend in-house from the 30kg sacks — zero new procurement, and loose/own-pack margin instead of a brand's.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Khichdi Mix, Tata Sampann khichdi mix, millet-dal khichdi blends
skuLines.notes: Three cohorts at once: babies past dal-water, the elderly, and hostel students with only a kettle or induction plate. Millet-pulse blends are a live 2026 launch trend.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Pulses Mix For Sprout, mixed-sprout packs (moong+moth+chana+lobia)
skuLines.notes: Blend it in-house from lines already stocked. Feeds the fresh-sprouts service at the F&V counter as well as home sprouters.

skuLines.examples: Rajdhani Besan, Tata Sampann Besan, Fortune Besan, Aashirvaad Besan
skuLines.seasonality: year-round; spikes in monsoon (pakoras) and at festivals (laddoo, barfi)
skuLines.notes: In a Punjabi kitchen besan is a weekly staple (kadhi, pakora, cheela), not an occasional buy — it turns faster than any single dal. Shelf life is shorter than whole pulses: ~4-6 months, and it absorbs moisture badly in a damp hill store. Buy small and often.

skuLines.line: Besan — loose / mill-fresh, ground on site
skuLines.examples: Loose besan ground from own chana dal, chakki-fresh besan
skuLines.notes: Rural and small-town buyers actively prefer being weighed in front of; pre-packed reads as stale or short-weight. Grinding own chana dal converts a nil-GST commodity into the highest-margin line in the aisle. Needs an FSSAI licence if labelled and packed.

skuLines.examples: Aashirvaad Chana Sattu, Skill Foods Roasted Chana Sattu, kala chana sattu atta
skuLines.seasonality: Apr-Jun (cooling drink); year-round for the protein buyers
skuLines.notes: A live 2026 launch category (ITC put Aashirvaad Chana Sattu into select markets). Cheap high-protein drink for students — pairs well with the canteen selling sattu sharbat.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Gram Roasted Whole, Good Life Roasted Chana, loose bhuna chana
skuLines.seasonality: year-round; peaks in winter and exam months
skuLines.notes: The best-margin, highest-frequency item in this whole category for a residential-school population: pocket-money priced, no cooking, no cold chain, protein-dense, and it fits the Rs 208 average bill. Stock Rs 10 and Rs 20 pouches at the Ary Lite counter, not just 500g.

skuLines.line: Roasted chana dal / split roasted gram (daliya chana)
skuLines.examples: Good Life Gram Roasted Split, Organic Tattva Roasted Chana Dal, loose roasted chana dal
skuLines.notes: Doubles as a namkeen base and as the grinding stock for chutney/sattu. Long shelf life, monsoon-safe.

skuLines.line: Moong dal badi / mangodi and urad wadi
skuLines.examples: Marwar Moong Dal Badi, Yuvraj Moong Mangodi, Kasbaa Urad Dal Masala Badi, local hand-made badi
skuLines.seasonality: cooked most in winter; traditionally made in summer
skuLines.notes: A dal-derived sabzi ingredient North Indian families genuinely miss when a store does not carry it — and there is no substitute. Fragile, so hill transit breakage is a real cost; buy in cartons, not loose sacks.

skuLines.examples: Lijjat urad papad, Lijjat moong papad, Bikaji papad, local hand-rolled papad
skuLines.notes: Dal-based and belongs beside the urad dals. Very breakage-prone on hill roads and it goes limp in monsoon humidity — small, frequent orders and airtight overwrap.

skuLines.examples: Nutrela Soya Chunks, Aashirvaad Soya Chunks, Fortune Soya Chunks, loose soya bari
skuLines.notes: The cheapest protein per rupee in the store and a mess/canteen workhorse — Aashirvaad Soya Chunks is called out as a high-growth line in ITC's own FY27 Q1 results. Light and non-perishable, so it is cheap to haul up the hill.

skuLines.examples: Nutrela Soya Granules, Fortune Soya Granules
skuLines.notes: Used as a mince extender (keema-style). One facing behind the chunks.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Raw Peanuts, loose mungfali, bb Royal Peanuts
skuLines.notes: A legume, and modern trade files it in the pulses aisle (Reliance Good Life does). Lohri and Maghi are big dates in a Punjabi Sikh township — peanut and gur demand spikes hard in January.

skuLines.examples: Good Life Peanut Roasted Skin Salted, Haldiram's peanuts, masala mungfali
skuLines.notes: Small-ticket, high-margin, fits the Ary Lite counter. Goes rancid faster than raw — rotate on date, especially through the humid months.

skuLines.examples: MTR Dal Makhani, Gits Dal Tadka, Haldiram's Chana Masala, ITC Kitchens of India dal bukhara
skuLines.seasonality: year-round; peaks in exam weeks and when the mess is closed
skuLines.notes: Retort pouches need no fridge and no cooking — the right answer for university hostellers with no kitchen and for staff on a late shift. Ambient shelf life 12-18 months makes them ideal for a store that indents monthly.

skuLines.line: Fried dal namkeen (moong dal, chana, mixture)
skuLines.examples: Haldiram's Moong Dal, Bikaji Moong Dal, Balaji chana dal namkeen, Bikano Navratan
skuLines.notes: Dal-based and, at Rs 5-20, the format that actually matches 7.2 bills a month from a school population. Volume driver for the Ary Lite counter; watch oil rancidity in summer.

skuLines.examples: Yoga Bar / Open Secret protein chips, Too Yumm chana chips, roasted-lentil protein snacks
skuLines.notes: Lentil/chickpea protein chips are the fastest-growing snack format globally and now on Indian shelves. Two or three SKUs only — university students and gym-going young staff, not the school children.

skuLines.line: Lentil / chickpea pasta and pulse noodles
skuLines.examples: Chana besan pasta, moong dal pasta, high-protein lentil fusilli
skuLines.notes: A 2026 premium-shelf experiment, not a staple. One or two facings; slow-moving if the price gap to regular pasta is wide.

skuLines.examples: 24 Mantra Organic, Organic Tattva, Tata Sampann Organic, bb Organic tur/moong/chana/masoor/rajma
skuLines.notes: Organic staples have reached q-commerce (Instamart's certified-organic range covers tur, rajma, masoor, kabuli). On this campus, restrict to toor, chana, moong, masoor and rajma — a full organic wall will not turn at Rs 1,493 per resident per month.

skuLines.line: Institutional sortex-clean bulk sacks (canteen and warehouse)
skuLines.examples: BigBasket Institutional Bulk Toor Dal 50kg, Institutional Chana Dal 25kg bag, Hyperpure Chana Dal 10kg, mill 30kg PP sacks
skuLines.seasonality: stock up May-Jun before the monsoon damages the hill road
skuLines.marginBand: 3-10% on internal transfer; 12-22% when broken to loose
skuLines.notes: BigBasket lists 50kg institutional toor at Rs 5,000 (Rs 100/kg). Two levers here: (1) packs ABOVE 25kg are GST-exempt, and dal broken from a 25kg+ sack and sold truly loose stays nil-rated — so the sack route is both cheaper and cleaner than buying 1kg branded; (2) it is the supply line for the two canteens and the F&V/Ary Lite counters. Counter-lever: pulse beetle completes a life cycle in 25-40 days at 30C/70% RH, so a monsoon-held sack can be a total loss — size the indent to 4-6 weeks of offtake, not a season.

skuLines.line: Subsidised / price-floor dal pack (government Bharat brand)
skuLines.examples: Bharat Dal chana dal, Bharat Moong Dal, Bharat Masoor Dal (NAFED / NCCF / Kendriya Bhandar channel)
skuLines.priceBand: Rs 60-90 per kg (VERIFY current notified rate and availability)
skuLines.notes: HONESTY FLAG: I could not verify this line — my web-search budget ran out before I could check the 2026 Bharat-brand price and whether the scheme is still running. Treat it as a lead to confirm with NAFED/NCCF, not a fact. If live, it is the cheapest way to hold a visible low price on chana dal for the lowest-paid non-teaching staff.

skuLines.line: Fresh sprouted moong and mixed sprouts (counter-made)
skuLines.examples: Own-made sprouted moong, mixed sprouts (moong+moth+chana), 200g/250g punnets
skuLines.notes: The only line in this category that needs cold chain: sprouts must be kept chilled and sold same-day or next-day, so run it off the F&V counter's refrigeration and sprout to a standing daily quantity. Highest value-add in the aisle — raw moong at ~Rs 140/kg becomes ~Rs 150-200/kg of sprouts by weight gain alone, plus the convenience premium. Needs an FSSAI hygiene protocol since it is a ready-to-eat item.

trends2026: Unpolished dal is now its own shelf tier, not a niche claim — Tata Sampann's whole range is positioned on 'no artificial polishing with water, oil or leather', and Reliance Good Life carries explicit 'Unpolished' variants of chana, moong, masoor and toor alongside the polished ones. A retailer is expected to stock both grades of the same dal.

Protein-first labelling: dal is being sold as India's cheapest protein with grams-per-serving on front-of-pack, and lentil/chickpea protein chips are described as the fastest-growing snack format in the world. High-protein Indian snack launches (roasted chana, moong dal, besan cheela mixes) are the visible end of it.

Value-added pulse derivatives are outgrowing raw dal: ITC's Q1 FY27 release calls out sustained high growth in Aashirvaad Besan and Aashirvaad Soya Chunks and the launch of Aashirvaad Chana Sattu in select markets — sattu in particular moved from a regional loose commodity to a branded packaged category.

Organic certified pulses have reached quick commerce: Swiggy Instamart now lists a certified-organic staples range (tur dal, rajma, masoor, kabuli chana), and Organic Tattva / 24 Mantra / Tata Sampann Organic sell through Blinkit and JioMart — so organic dal is no longer a specialty-store-only tier.

Sortex/laser-cleaned and calibre-graded stock is being stated as a retail claim ('sortex clean', bold 7mm+, Madhi grade, 'restaurant grade' toor), splitting one variety into two or three price points on the same shelf.

Institutional bulk packs are sold openly through modern trade and B2B, not just mandis — BigBasket lists 25kg and 50kg institutional toor and chana dal, Hyperpure sells 10kg packs — and because pre-packaged-and-labelled GST at 5% applies only up to 25kg, packs above 25kg stay exempt, which is quietly reshaping how institutions buy.

Origin-named regional pulses as premium: Chamba Kugti rajma, Bharmour rajma and pahari kulth/gahat are sold at multiples of commodity price by hill-focused brands (Pahaari Bazar, Buraansh, Kumaon Foods) — the same premiumisation logic that hit rice and spices is now hitting pulses.

Millet-pulse convenience blends (khichdi mixes, dal-millet combos, tadka mixes, sprout mixes) are a growing sub-shelf, driven by the mixed-dal market's convenience-led growth and by smaller urban households not wanting five open dal jars.
adjacentServices: Weigh-and-pack loose counter — break 30kg sacks and weigh in front of the customer. Rural and small-town buyers actively distrust pre-packed pouches as stale or short-weight, and loose sale is GST-nil while carrying 15-30% margin versus 2-8% on branded packs. The single highest-value service in this category.

On-site grinding: besan from own chana dal, sattu from roasted chana, and coarse dal grinding for baby food. Converts a nil-rated commodity into the best-margin line in the aisle with no new procurement. Needs an FSSAI licence and Legal Metrology declarations the moment output is labelled and packed.
In-house blends the campus actually eats: a maa-chole (urad chilka + chana dal) langar blend, a panchratna mix, a sprouting mix, a khichdi mix — all made from sacks already in the warehouse.

Canteen and mess supply contract from the warehouse at a published per-kg list, indenting 25kg+ sacks (GST-exempt above 25kg) instead of retail packs. Two canteens plus the F&V and Ary Lite counters give the store a captive B2B leg that stabilises pulse offtake.

Monthly staple ration kit for staff families (dal + atta + rice + oil + besan) on standing order, optionally settled against salary. Fixes the demand forecast, which is what makes pre-monsoon bulk buying safe.

Pest-proof storage attach-on: sell airtight/opaque dal containers and neem or bay-leaf sachets beside the loose counter, and offer a 'monsoon pack' (smaller quantity + sachet). An open dal bag infests within 2-3 weeks at monsoon humidity, so this is a real service, not an upsell.

Free re-cleaning / winnowing of infested household stock, and a no-argument replacement policy on weevil-hit dal. In a captive township where the customer cannot go elsewhere, trust on this one issue is worth more than the margin lost.

Daily sprouting service off the F&V counter's chiller — sprouted moong and mixed sprouts made from raw stock already held, the highest value-add in the category. Requires same-day/next-day sale and an FSSAI hygiene protocol as a ready-to-eat item.
Pre-soaked and pre-cooked dal/chole for hostel students and single staff with no kitchen; and a small retort-pouch shelf for exam weeks and mess-closed days.

Pre-monsoon advance indent (take orders in May-June for the year's rajma, chana and kabuli before the hill road deteriorates), balanced against a 4-6 week weevil-risk ceiling on how much can safely be held.
Local farmer procurement in Sirmaur, Chamba and Rajgarh for rajma, kulth and bhatt — a premium local shelf, shorter supply line than Delhi/Indore, and a story a Trust-run store can legitimately own.
In-campus delivery of 5kg and heavier packs to staff quarters, which is what unlocks larger basket sizes against the current Rs 208 average bill.
